kurz: The purchase price is only one of three amounts that decide a property purchase, and the only one shown in the listing.

bloecke.md: Three amounts decide a property deal. The first is the purchase price shown in the listing. The second is the incidental purchase costs. They fall due within a few weeks of notarisation, are irretrievably lost once paid and do not reappear in any valuation of the property. The third amount is maintenance. It arises over decades, is not in any contract and is not invoiced by anyone, which is why it is regularly set at zero. Over the useful life, it adds up to a multiple of the incidental purchase costs.

## One-off incidental purchase costs

[[Real estate transfer tax (Grunderwerbsteuer)]] is usually the largest item and can no more be negotiated than the costs of the notary and land register. Under Section 13 GrEStG (Real Estate Transfer Tax Act), both parties to the contract owe the tax as joint and several debtors; in the purchase contract, it is practically always imposed on the buyer. Since the 2006 federalism reform, the tax rate has been a matter for the federal states (Article 105(2a) GG, Basic Law), and the standard federal rate of 3.5% in Section 11 GrEStG now only applies in Bavaria. The notary reports the contract to the tax office. The tax assessment notice arrives after a few weeks and must be paid one month later (Section 15 GrEStG). Only then does the tax office issue the clearance certificate (Unbedenklichkeitsbescheinigung), without which the land registry will not register the transfer of ownership (Section 22 GrEStG). The payment therefore cannot be postponed, because without it the buyer does not become the owner.

bloecke.titel: Real estate transfer tax by federal state, as of 2026
zeilen: Baden-Württemberg, Lower Saxony, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia

bloecke.md:
Between Bavaria and Brandenburg, the difference is twelve thousand euros, for the same property at the same price, purely because of the state border. In 2024, Thuringia became the only state so far to lower its rate again, from 6.5% to 5.0%.

The costs of the notary and land register together amount to around 1% to 1.5% of the purchase price, depending on the amount of the land charge (Grundschuld). The fees are laid down in the Court and Notary Fees Act (GNotKG), depend on the transaction value and are not negotiable. A notary who granted a discount would be committing a breach of official duty. The fees essentially cover the notarisation of the purchase contract, the priority notice of conveyance (Auflassungsvormerkung), the registration of the transfer of ownership and the registration of the land charge for the bank.

The estate agent's fee, the **commission** (Courtage), is the only negotiable item. Since the Act on the Distribution of Estate Agent Costs (Gesetz über die Verteilung der Maklerkosten) of 12 June 2020, in force since 23 December 2020 (Sections 656a to 656d BGB, Civil Code), an estate agency contract for the purchase of a flat or a single-family house must be in text form. If the buyer is a consumer, they may bear at most half of the commission. In addition, their obligation to pay only falls due once the party who engaged the agent has demonstrably paid its share. The law does not regulate the amount itself. The usual rate is 3.57% per side including VAT, so up to 7.14% in total. The commission is nevertheless negotiable, and in weak markets it is negotiated.

bloecke.titel: From purchase price to all-in cost
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for a purchase price of €400,000 in North Rhine-Westphalia, with 1.5% for the notary and land register and the halved commission of 3.57%. The incidental costs amount to €46,280 or 11.6% of the purchase price.

bloecke.md:
The bank bases the loan on the mortgage lending value of the property, not on the total costs of the purchase. Real estate transfer tax, notary, land register and commission do not increase the value of the property and must therefore be paid from equity. Buyers who finance them as well start with a loan-to-value ratio above 100% and pay a noticeable interest rate premium for it over the entire fixed-rate period.

In the example, a buyer with €100,000 in equity has €53,720 left for the purchase price after the notary appointment. The loan requirement is therefore €346,280 instead of €300,000, which is just over 86% of the purchase price.

bloecke.titel: Market value and all-in cost over time
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation based on the all-in cost of €446,280. At the most recently measured pace of the house price index (+0.6% in the second quarter of 2026 compared with the previous year), the market value only reaches it after just over 18 years; at the pace of the fourth quarter of 2025 (+2.6%), after just over four.

bloecke.md:
The chart is an arithmetical check, not a forecast. As long as the market value is below the dashed line, a sale would mean a loss, even if the price has risen. Estate agent's costs on resale are not yet included. Because a sale before this point is expensive, owning property is illiquid.

One qualification applies to a let property. There, the incidental costs are not entirely lost, because they form part of the acquisition costs. To the extent that they are attributable to the building, they are deducted through depreciation under Section 7 EStG (Income Tax Act). The part attributable to the land is left out there as well. For owner-occupiers, the amount brings no tax relief at all.

## Running costs

[[Property tax (Grundsteuer)]] has been levied under new rules since 1 January 2025. In the federal model, it is calculated as property tax value (Grundsteuerwert) times tax base rate (Steuermesszahl) times the municipality's multiplier (Hebesatz); for residential properties, a base rate of 0.31 per mille applies. A property tax value of €250,000 results in a tax base amount of €77.50; with a multiplier of 500%, that is €387.50 a year. Baden-Württemberg, Bavaria, Hamburg, Hesse and Lower Saxony calculate according to their own state models. The reform was designed to be revenue-neutral for each municipality, that is, to raise the same total tax revenue. This aim did not apply to the individual plot, where the tax may have risen or fallen considerably.

In addition, there are residential buildings insurance and liability insurance, the chimney sweep, water, waste water, refuse, street cleaning, electricity for common areas and, for a flat, the service charge (Hausgeld) paid to the community of owners. For the calculation, what matters most is who ultimately bears these items, and less their amount. Section 2 of the Operating Costs Ordinance (BetrKV) lists exhaustively which costs may be passed on to a tenant; Section 1(2) BetrKV expressly excludes two items.

bloecke.md: For owner-occupiers, this split has no practical significance, because they pay both columns themselves. However, it explains why the gross rent of an investment property and the cost burden of an owner-occupied home are two different figures. It also shows why the items in the right-hand column are missing from every yield calculation that looks too good.

## Maintenance and reserves

A building wears out. Roof, windows, heating, pipes and wiring, facade and bathrooms have a limited lifespan, and the costs of renewing them arise irregularly, each time in five-figure amounts. Whether money has been set aside for this or not makes no difference to when they fall due. For a flat, Section 19(2) no. 4 WEG (Apartment Ownership Act) requires the community of owners to keep an appropriate [[Maintenance reserve (Erhaltungsrücklage)|maintenance reserve (Erhaltungsrücklage)]]. The law does not specify what is appropriate.

There are two competing conventions for the amount. The official one is in Section 28 of the Second Computation Ordinance. Since 1 January 2026, it has set the following per square metre of living space per year: €11.50 for a building under 22 years old, €14.58 for 22 to 31 years and €18.62 from 32 years; with a lift, a surcharge is added. The original values from 2002 (€7.10, €9.00 and €11.50) have been adjusted to the consumer price index every three years since 2005. These rates formally apply only to price-controlled housing, but are generally used as a calculation parameter. The second convention comes from the construction industry and is cited as the Peters formula (Petersche Formel).

bloecke.formel: Reserve per year = Construction costs × 1.5 / 80 = 1.875% of construction costs
bloecke.erklaerung: The Peters formula assumes that over a useful life of 80 years, maintenance costs of one and a half times the original construction costs are incurred. It is a rule of thumb from the literature, not a legal standard.
variablen: building costs only, excluding the plot, not the purchase price
factor for the entire renewal requirement over the useful life
bloecke.beispiel: 80 m² at assumed construction costs of €2,500 per square metre gives €200,000. 1.875% of this is €3,750 a year. In the literature on the WEG, 65% to 70% of this is usually allocated to the common property, that is, around €2,440 to €2,625. The rest, for bathroom, floors and interior fittings, is attributable to the separate property (Sondereigentum) and therefore to the owner alone.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for 80 m², a purchase price of €400,000, assumed construction costs of €2,500 per square metre and the II. BV rates from 2026. Between the official flat rate and the rules of thumb there is a factor of 2.5 to 4.3, which is why every figure quoted needs a statement of which convention is meant.
kategorien: Section 28 II. BV, building under 22 years
Section 28 II. BV, 32 years and older
Rule of thumb: 1% of purchase price

bloecke.md: There are arguments for both conventions. The II. BV rates were derived empirically from the stock of publicly subsidised rental housing and cover maintenance, but not modernisation. A new heating system, facade insulation or the installation of a lift are not provided for in them. The Peters formula extrapolates the building's complete renewal cycle and is therefore systematically higher. On the other hand, it relies on the construction costs, which nobody knows exactly for an existing property. In practice, the reserve of a community of owners that follows Section 28 II. BV is therefore sufficient for ongoing repairs, but not for the first major renovation.

A low reserve does not lower the costs; it postpones them. The missing amount is made up through a special levy (Sonderumlage), in one sum and on a date that the owner does not determine. This typically happens when construction prices are high as well. Construction prices for residential buildings rose by around 89% between 2010 and 2025 and in May 2026 were again 5.0% above the previous year.

There is no official checklist, but there is a useful order. What to ask for is the year of the last renewal, not the condition, in each case with written evidence:

- Heating system, hot water supply and heat distribution
- Roof covering including gutters and chimney head
- Windows and front door, with details of the glazing
- Electrics, with the meter cabinet, cable cross-sections and number of circuits
- Risers for water and waste water, the most common cause of unexpectedly high costs in old buildings
- Facade, thermal insulation, balconies and their waterproofing

Common empirical values from lifespan tables are two decades for a heating system, three to four decades for windows and bathrooms and four to six decades for a roof. If several components reach the end of their lifespan at the same time, the costs add up. A property whose components all date from the same decade is therefore riskier than one that has been worked on in stages.

## Energy performance certificate and legal obligations

When a property is sold, an energy performance certificate is mandatory under the Building Modernisation Act (GModG), as the Buildings Energy Act (Gebäudeenergiegesetz) has been called since 29 July 2026. It must be presented unprompted at the viewing at the latest and handed over without delay after the purchase contract has been concluded (Section 80(4) GModG). It is valid for ten years (Section 79 GModG), and its key figures must already appear in the property advertisement (Section 87 GModG). If it is missing, that is an administrative offence. Under civil law, this usually has no consequences, but it does allow conclusions to be drawn about the seller.

For estimating costs, what matters is which of the two types of energy performance certificate is available. The **consumption-based certificate** (Verbrauchsausweis) evaluates the heating bills of the last three years and thus measures the heating habits of the previous occupants. A frugal couple who heated only two of five rooms will therefore produce a good rating even in a poor house. The **demand-based certificate** (Bedarfsausweis) is calculated from the building envelope, windows and building services and does not depend on the occupants' behaviour. Only this type is suitable as a forecast. If a consumption-based certificate is available, the gas or oil consumption of the last three years in kilowatt hours is the better information, and asking for it costs nothing.

The GModG requires insulation of an insufficiently insulated ceiling of the top storey (Section 35 GModG) and of previously uninsulated, accessible heating and hot water pipes in unheated rooms (Section 69 GModG). The former ban on operating oil and gas constant-temperature boilers more than 30 years old was dropped with the new version in July 2026.

The well-known exemption for one- and two-family houses applies only to owners who were already living in the house themselves on 1 February 2002. It lapses on sale. The purchaser must meet the obligations within two years of the transfer of ownership. If a seller correctly says they never had to retrofit anything, they are only describing their own situation, not that of the buyer.

Also dropped is the requirement to run a newly installed heating system on at least 65% renewable energy. If a new gas, oil or liquefied petroleum gas heating system is installed in an existing building after 29 July 2026, a rising share of the heat must come from biogenic fuels or hydrogen: at least 10% from 2029 and at least 60% from 2040 (Section 43 GModG). This part of the law has been politically contested since 2023 and was fundamentally changed in 2026. Before deciding to buy, the current legal position should be checked, instead of relying on the memory of a headline.

- current land register extract with sections II and III (rights of way, rights of residence, land charges) and information from the register of contaminated sites
- energy performance certificate, with attention to the type of certificate and the date of issue
- evidence of the year of the last renewal of the six expensive components
- for a flat, also the declaration of division (Teilungserklärung), the budget, the level of the maintenance reserve and the minutes of the last three owners' meetings
- your own calculation of the incidental costs with the real estate transfer tax rate of the correct federal state
- a fixed item for maintenance in the household budget that stays there even when nothing is broken

mitnehmen: Depending on the federal state and whether an estate agent is involved, incidental purchase costs are between around 4.5% and just under 12% of the purchase price; they do not increase the mortgage lending value, are lost immediately and must come from equity.
With a purchase price of €400,000, a difference of twelve thousand euros arises solely from which side of a state border the property is on.
There are two competing conventions for maintenance, which differ by a factor of 2.5 to 4; Section 28 II. BV covers ongoing repairs, the Peters formula the full renewal cycle.
Under Section 1(2) BetrKV, management and maintenance are never recoverable from tenants and are therefore missing from every overly optimistic yield calculation.

The retrofit obligations under Sections 35 and 69 GModG (until July 2026 the Buildings Energy Act) transfer with ownership, because the previous owner's exemption lapses on sale; the buyer has two years to carry out the retrofit.

begriffe.text: Real estate transfer tax, notary and land register costs and estate agent's commission, depending on the federal state and whether an estate agent is involved around 4.5% to just under 12% of the purchase price. They arise immediately after the purchase and do not increase the value of the property. For owner-occupiers, they are also lost for tax purposes.

State tax on the acquisition of a property, in 2026 between 3.5% (Bavaria) and 6.5% (Brandenburg, North Rhine-Westphalia, Saarland, Schleswig-Holstein). Only after it has been paid does the tax office issue the clearance certificate, without which no entry is made in the land register (Section 22 GrEStG).

Amount that a community of owners must build up for future maintenance; Section 19(2) no. 4 WEG requires an appropriate level. The law does not put a figure on this level. A reserve that is too low shifts the costs into a later special levy.

Rule of thumb for calculating maintenance, according to which 1.5 times the construction costs are incurred over 80 years, that is, 1.875% a year. It is not a legal standard and is systematically above the rates in Section 28 II. BV, because it includes the full renewal cycle.

Energy performance certificate whose rating is calculated from the building envelope, windows and building services and therefore does not depend on the occupants' heating habits. Its counterpart is the consumption-based certificate, which evaluates the bills of the last three years.
